documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT. 53M, parts manager at an auto supply, here to set up primary care. Old PCP retired; he has been getting refills through the GI office and urgent care in between.

Liver: told he had cirrhosis at his first bleed in Sept 2020 — vomited blood at work, admitted, scoped and banded. Second bleed this March, banded again. Both admissions at an outside hospital. Followed by an outside GI group, last seen there in the spring. On furosemide and spironolactone for fluid, propranolol since the first bleed. Also takes vitamin K daily and lactulose when constipated. Has known he has hep C for years (brother has it too) and was never treated; says nobody ever pushed it.

Alcohol: honest about it. Six beers a night most nights, has been that way about 15 years. Cut back for a few weeks after each admission and drifted back. Not interested in a program right now. Former smoker, quit 2016.

Hormones: says he was told as a teenager his body didn't make enough testosterone and has been on shots ever since. Injects 200 mg every 2 weeks at home. For about 4 months his interest in sex is way down and erections are unreliable. Wants it looked at.

PSH: umbilical hernia as a kid. EGD with banding x2.
FH: father died at 58 of alcoholic cirrhosis and liver cancer. Mother living, HTN and high cholesterol. Brother with chronic hep C. Paternal uncle drank heavily.
Allergies: none known.
Immunizations per pt: tetanus shot 2016, two COVID shots this spring. Doesn't recall any others.

Exam: thin man, looks older than stated age. BP 104/64 HR 62. Sclerae anicteric in this light. Palmar erythema. A few spider angiomata on the upper chest. Lungs clear. RRR. Abdomen distended, fluid wave present, nontender. No asterixis. Trace ankle edema.

A/P
1. Alcoholic cirrhosis with portal hypertension and ascites, 2 prior banded variceal bleeds. Continue furosemide 40, spironolactone 100, propranolol 20 bid. CMP/CBC/INR today. Records requested from the hospital and old PCP. Liver US every 6 months for cancer screening given cirrhosis and his father's history — first one ordered.
2. Chronic hepatitis C, untreated. Referring to ID for treatment; cure would matter for him.
3. Alcohol use disorder. AUDIT-C 10. Talked plainly about what alcohol is doing to his liver and the bleeding risk. Offered referral to addiction medicine and a medicine to help with cravings; he declined both today but listened. Will keep asking.
4. Hypogonadism on testosterone, now low libido and ED. Liver disease and alcohol are likely part of it. Endocrinology referral to sort out what we're dealing with.
5. HIV screen today, he agreed.
6. Return 3 months, sooner if any bleeding, black stools, confusion or rapid belly swelling — go straight to the ED for vomiting blood.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Mr. Cummings, your labs from yesterday are back. Your liver numbers are what I expected with cirrhosis and active hep C — the liver enzymes are elevated, bilirubin is up and albumin (a protein the liver makes) is low. Your platelets are low, which goes with an enlarged spleen from the pressure in the liver's veins, and you are mildly anemic. Kidney function and sodium look fine on the water pills. HIV test negative. Nothing here changes the plan. I've added the low platelets and anemia to your list so we can track them.

Discharge summary, admission 9/14/2020 to 9/18/2020. Presented with hematemesis. New diagnosis of cirrhosis, felt to be alcohol related with hepatitis C contributing. EGD: esophageal varices with stigmata of recent bleeding, band ligation performed. Discharged on propranolol 20 mg twice daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, spironolactone 100 mg daily, vitamin K, lactulose as needed. Advised complete abstinence. Allergies: no known drug allergies.

Discharge summary, admission 3/2/2021 to 3/5/2021. Recurrent upper GI bleed. EGD with band ligation of esophageal varices. Home medications resumed unchanged. GI follow-up arranged.

Prior PCP: last visit 2019. Tdap 5/2016. Testosterone cypionate continued from an endocrinologist he saw years ago, refills by PCP. No colonoscopy on file.

reports.text: Indication: cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance. The liver has a nodular contour and coarse echotexture. No focal hepatic lesion. Main portal vein patent with hepatopetal flow. No intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary dilation. Gallbladder unremarkable. Spleen enlarged. Ascites present in the abdomen. Kidneys normal in size without hydronephrosis.
reports.conclusion: Cirrhotic liver without focal lesion. Splenomegaly and ascites.

documents.title: Endocrinology consultation
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE ENDOCRINOLOGY CONSULTATION — date of visit 08/02/2021, received 08/09/2021.

Reason for referral: low libido and erectile dysfunction in a man on testosterone replacement.

History: 53-year-old man, referred by his primary care physician. Over roughly the last six months he has noticed reduced sexual desire and difficulty with erections. He was evaluated as an adolescent for absent pubertal development and has taken testosterone since; current dose testosterone cypionate 200 mg intramuscularly every 2 weeks, self-administered, no missed doses. Background of cirrhosis from alcohol with portal hypertension and prior variceal bleeding, and untreated hepatitis C. Drinks about six beers daily.

Medications: furosemide 40 mg daily, spironolactone 100 mg daily, propranolol 20 mg twice daily, testosterone cypionate 200 mg IM every 2 weeks, vitamin K 10 mg daily, lactulose 30 mL twice daily as needed.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Family history: father deceased at 58, alcoholic cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; mother with hypertension and hyperlipidemia; brother with hepatitis C; paternal uncle with alcohol use disorder.

Examination: undernourished-appearing. Palmar erythema. Spider angiomata across the chest. Abdomen distended with a fluid wave. Genital exam with small, atrophic testes.

Laboratory: albumin 2.9 g/dL, total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 120 U/L, AST 180 U/L, ALT 150 U/L, INR 1.6. Estradiol elevated.

Assessment: His history is that of Kallmann syndrome, congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, appropriately treated with testosterone for decades. The new symptoms are best explained by additional factors: advanced liver disease, ongoing alcohol use and excess estrogen from the liver disease, reflected in the elevated estradiol. His hypogonadism is now multifactorial.

Plan: continue testosterone cypionate 200 mg every 2 weeks without change. The most effective step for his symptoms is stopping alcohol; discussed directly. No additional medication recommended at this time. Return as needed.

Thank you for this referral.

Allergies reviewed: NKDA.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:

He took that better than I expected. Still drinking, "maybe five most nights now." No bleeding, no black stools. Belly about the same. ID appointment is next month.
O: BP 102/66 HR 60. Thin. Palmar erythema. Abdomen distended with fluid wave, nontender. No asterixis. Trace ankle edema.
A/P:
- Kallmann syndrome per endocrinology; on list. Testosterone unchanged, refills here.
- Cirrhosis/portal HTN/ascites: stable. Same diuretics and propranolol. Labs today.
- AUD: again offered addiction medicine or medication. Not yet. "Let me get through the hep C stuff first."
- Flu vaccine given L deltoid.
- Return in 3 months.

documents.title: Infectious Diseases consultation
documents.author: infectious diseases
documents.body:
INFECTIOUS DISEASES CLINIC — NEW CONSULT. Seen 10/12/2021, letter sent 10/19/2021.

Referred for treatment of chronic hepatitis C. He has known about the infection for several years and has never been treated. Cirrhosis with ascites on diuretics and two prior variceal bleeds (2020, 2021). Drinks daily. No injection drug use.

Allergies: NKDA. Medications reviewed: furosemide, spironolactone, propranolol, testosterone cypionate, vitamin K, lactulose PRN. No interactions of concern with sofosbuvir/velpatasvir.

Exam: thin, mild ascites, palmar erythema.

Data: HCV RNA 1,850,000 IU/mL. Genotype 1a.

Impression: chronic HCV genotype 1a with decompensated cirrhosis (ascites, prior variceal hemorrhage).

Plan: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir 400/100 mg one tablet daily. Ribavirin would usually be added for decompensated disease, but he is already anemic; we will give 24 weeks without ribavirin instead. Prior authorization submitted. HCV RNA at end of treatment and 12 weeks after. Ongoing alcohol use does not prevent treatment but we encouraged him to stop. Liver care remains with his gastroenterologist.

documents.title: Gastroenterology clinic note
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
GASTROENTEROLOGY FOLLOW-UP — visit 1/26/2022, faxed 1/31/2022.

Known to our clinic for cirrhosis. Since his endocrine evaluation last summer he has noticed bright red blood with stools for several weeks — streaks on tissue, some in the water. He also mentions intermittent abdominal fullness, ankle swelling and bruising easily. Over the past few months he has felt progressively more tired and gets mildly short of breath with exertion. No abdominal pain, no diarrhea, no recent travel. Currently on sofosbuvir/velpatasvir through ID.

Meds: furosemide 40, spironolactone 100, propranolol 20 BID, testosterone cypionate 200 mg q2wk, vitamin K 10 mg, lactulose PRN, sofosbuvir/velpatasvir. NKDA.

Exam: chronically ill appearance. Scleral icterus. Spider angiomas over the chest. Mild ascites. Spleen tip palpable below the left costal margin. Bilateral ankle edema. Rectal: no external lesions or fissure; stool guaiac positive.

Labs: platelets low, mild anemia, INR elevated, transaminases elevated — consistent with his prior values.
Ultrasound today: nodular liver consistent with cirrhosis.
Anoscopy in clinic: engorged internal hemorrhoidal veins in the distal rectum, no active bleeding.

Impression: symptomatic internal hemorrhoids in the setting of portal hypertension and thrombocytopenia.
Plan: colonoscopy to exclude another source given occult blood, then rubber band ligation in clinic. Continue current medications. Avoid straining; lactulose as needed.

documents.title: Colonoscopy report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
COLONOSCOPY — 2/14/2022, report received 2/16.
Indication: hematochezia, positive occult blood, cirrhosis.
Sedation: monitored anesthesia care. Prep: good.
Cecum reached and confirmed by appendiceal orifice and ileocecal valve; terminal ileum not entered. Withdrawal time 9 minutes.
Findings: Colon mucosa normal throughout. No polyps, masses, diverticula or vascular lesions. Retroflexion shows non-bleeding internal hemorrhoids.
Impression: internal hemorrhoids, otherwise normal exam.
Recommendation: proceed with hemorrhoid banding in clinic. Next colonoscopy in 10 years. NKDA.

documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body: Office procedure 3/7/2022. Rubber band ligation of internal hemorrhoids. Consent obtained. Anoscopy, single band applied to the largest column without pain. Tolerated well. Expect some fullness for a day or two and a small amount of blood when the band falls off. Second session in 4 weeks. NKDA.

documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
GI CLINIC — 2/6/2023, note faxed 2/10/2023.

Seen a year after his hemorrhoid workup. Two months of gradually worsening abdominal swelling and discomfort. Eating less. Denies nausea, vomiting or a change in bowel habits. No travel, no ill contacts. Adherent to furosemide and spironolactone. Ongoing alcohol use.

Meds: furosemide 40 daily, spironolactone 100 daily, propranolol 20 BID, testosterone cypionate 200 mg IM q2wk, vitamin K 10 mg daily, lactulose PRN. NKDA.

Exam: cachectic. Palmar erythema. Abdomen distended with fluid wave and shifting dullness. No peripheral edema today.

Labs: albumin 2.8, sodium 135, creatinine 1.1, total bilirubin 3.2, INR 1.5.

Procedure: diagnostic paracentesis, left lower quadrant, ultrasound-marked, after consent. Clear straw-colored fluid. Ascitic albumin 1.2 g/dL; serum-ascites albumin gradient 1.6, consistent with portal hypertension. Cell count without evidence of infection. No complications.

Impression: alcohol-related cirrhosis with portal hypertensive ascites; recent PCP ultrasound without liver lesion.
Plan: continue current diuretic doses — his blood pressure limits increases. Two-gram sodium diet reviewed. Abstinence strongly advised. Return in one year or sooner if needed.

documents.author: infectious diseases
documents.body:
ID CLINIC — annual visit 1/29/2024, letter 2/5/2024.

Following for hepatitis C, treated with sofosbuvir/velpatasvir in 2021–22 with sustained virologic response, on a background of alcohol-related cirrhosis with portal hypertension, Kallmann syndrome and internal hemorrhoids (banded 2022). He has no acute concerns; some fatigue now and then. He continues to drink daily.

Meds: furosemide, spironolactone, vitamin K, propranolol 20 mg BID, testosterone cypionate 200 mg IM every 2 weeks, lactulose 30 mL BID PRN. NKDA.

Vitals stable. Exam: mild ascites. Spider angiomas on the upper trunk; palmar erythema.

Labs: platelets 110,000, INR 1.2, albumin 3.2, total bilirubin 2.1, AST 80, ALT 75. HCV RNA not detected. Hepatitis B surface antigen negative, surface antibody negative.

Immunizations: tetanus booster 8 years ago (2016). No record of hepatitis A, hepatitis B or pneumococcal vaccination.

Assessment: HCV remains cured. Cirrhosis with no immunity to hepatitis B and no record of hepatitis A or pneumococcal vaccine.
Recommendations to primary care: hepatitis A series, hepatitis B series and a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV20). Tdap due in 2026. We will see him again only if needed; repeat HCV RNA if there is any new exposure.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Annual visit.

Interval: ID in January — hep C still cured, flagged his vaccine gaps; PCV20 and hep A/B series started here in Feb/March. No bleeding. Belly up and down with salt. Fatigue in the afternoons. Still 6 beers a night, AUDIT-C 10. Not interested in treatment; "I know, I know." PHQ-2 1.

Exam: BP 98/62, HR 64, afebrile, weight about the same. Chronically ill-looking, thin arms. Faint scleral yellowing in daylight. Spider angiomata chest, palmar erythema. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen distended, fluid wave, nontender. 1+ ankle edema. No asterixis, alert and oriented.

Vaccines: hep A #2 and hep B #3 today — both series complete.

Plan:
- Cirrhosis/portal HTN/ascites: continue regimen. Labs and AFP drawn today; US ordered for this week.
- Kallmann syndrome: testosterone level, Hct, PSA.
- AUD: remains the main driver. Discussed again what continued drinking means for bleeding and liver failure, and that I'm here when he is ready.
- RTC November.

GASTROENTEROLOGY — clinic visit 2/4/2025, faxed 2/10/2025.

He returns for cirrhosis follow-up; last seen here for ascites in 2023 and monitored since with his PCP's labs and surveillance imaging. Over two months his abdomen has grown and he fills up after a few bites. No change in diet or bowels.

Medications: furosemide 40 mg daily, spironolactone 100 mg daily, propranolol 20 mg twice daily, testosterone cypionate 200 mg IM every 2 weeks, vitamin K 10 mg daily, lactulose 30 mL twice daily as needed. NKDA.
Social: former smoker, quit about 8 years ago. Continues about six beers daily. Works as an automotive parts manager.
PMH includes chronic hepatitis C (treated), Kallmann syndrome, internal hemorrhoids.

Exam: numerous spider angiomas over the chest, palmar erythema, mild jaundice. Fluid wave and shifting dullness. Asterixis present.

Labs: albumin 2.8, total bilirubin 3.2, INR 1.6, platelets 95,000, AST 120, ALT 90. AFP normal.
Ultrasound: nodular liver contour, splenomegaly, ascites; no liver lesion.

Impression: decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis with portal hypertension and ascites.
Plan: continue current medications. Sodium restriction. Alcohol cessation — again strongly advised. Follow up in 6 months with labs and imaging.

GI CLINIC NOTE — visit 8/1/2025, received 8/6/2025.

Cirrhosis follow-up. For two months the abdomen has been steadily enlarging and uncomfortable, much as in 2023 and earlier this year. Poor appetite, early fullness. Denies fever, vomiting or change in stool. Known chronic hepatitis C history.

Social: former smoker (quit 8 years ago); about 6 beers a day; automotive parts manager.
Family: father died at 58 with alcoholic cirrhosis and HCC; mother with HTN and hyperlipidemia; brother with chronic hepatitis C; paternal uncle with alcohol use disorder.

Exam: cachectic. Jaundice of skin and sclerae. Fluid wave with shifting dullness. Pitting edema of the lower legs.

Labs: hemoglobin 10.2, platelets 85,000, INR 1.6, albumin 2.8, total bilirubin 3.2, creatinine 1.1, sodium 133. Urine sodium 5.
Imaging: ultrasound with flow study shows cirrhosis, splenomegaly and ascites, no portal vein thrombosis.

Assessment: ascites due to cirrhosis, uncomplicated.
Plan: same medications. Sodium restriction reinforced. Follow up in 6 months, sooner as needed.

documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT — regional hospital. Arrived 1/31/2026 by ambulance. Received by fax 2/9/2026.

CC: vomiting blood, black stools.
HPI: 57-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and portal hypertension, two prior variceal bleeds treated with banding (2020 and 2021). Vomited bright red blood twice this evening after a day of tarry stools. Abdomen more swollen with early satiety for some weeks.
Meds: furosemide 40 mg daily, spironolactone 100 mg daily, propranolol 20 mg BID, testosterone cypionate 200 mg IM q2wk, vitamin K 10 mg daily, lactulose PRN. NKDA.
Social: former smoker; drinks about 6 beers daily; parts manager.
Vitals: BP 92/58, HR 108, RR 18.
Exam: pale, lethargic but answering questions. Abdomen distended with fluid wave; dilated veins around the umbilicus.
Labs: hemoglobin 7.8, platelets 72,000, AST 68, ALT 44, total bilirubin 3.2, albumin 2.7, INR 1.8.
ED course: two large-bore IVs, octreotide infusion, ceftriaxone, transfusion started. GI and hepatology consulted. Admitted to the ICU step-down unit.

documents.title: Discharge summary: variceal hemorrhage, TIPS
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY — admitted 1/31/2026, discharged 2/5/2026. Received 2/9/2026.

Principal diagnosis: acute esophageal variceal hemorrhage due to portal hypertension in alcohol-related cirrhosis.

Hospital course: Resuscitated with 2 units packed red cells. Octreotide infusion and ceftriaxone prophylaxis. Urgent EGD the night of admission: esophageal varices, one with stigmata of active bleeding; band ligation performed with hemostasis. Given a third variceal bleed despite banding and beta-blockade, hepatology recommended a portosystemic shunt to lower portal pressure. Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt placed 2/2/2026 via right internal jugular access without complication. Hemoglobin stable afterward without further transfusion. No encephalopathy during the stay. Octreotide completed; antibiotic course completed in hospital.

Alcohol: counseled at length by the team and social work; he states he intends to stop. Outpatient resources provided.

Discharge medications: furosemide 40 mg daily, spironolactone 100 mg daily, testosterone cypionate 200 mg IM every 2 weeks, vitamin K 10 mg daily, lactulose 30 mL BID PRN. STOPPED: propranolol (not needed after TIPS).
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: hepatology clinic in 2–3 weeks with TIPS ultrasound; primary care within 2 weeks.

documents.author: RN
documents.body: Called after hospital records came in (variceal bleed, TIPS 2/2, propranolol stopped). Pt home, says he feels "wiped out but okay." No further bleeding, stools now brown. No confusion per pt. Hepatology appointment 2/23. Offered a post-discharge visit with PCP this week or next; he'd rather see hepatology first and will call us after. Reviewed ED precautions. Routed to PCP.

documents.title: Emergency department note
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT — regional hospital, 7/26/2026. Faxed 8/7/2026.

CC: leg swelling and abdominal distension.
HPI: 58M with alcohol-related cirrhosis, portal hypertension, prior variceal bleeding with TIPS placed in February. Two weeks of steadily increasing swelling of both legs and of the abdomen. Denies drinking any alcohol recently. No vomiting blood or black stools.
Home meds per patient list: furosemide 40 mg daily, spironolactone 100 mg daily, propranolol 20 mg BID, testosterone cypionate 200 mg IM q2wk, vitamin K 10 mg daily, lactulose PRN. NKDA.
PMH per records: chronic hepatitis C, Kallmann syndrome, hemorrhoids.
Vitals: BP 90/60, HR 102, temp 38.0 C.
Exam: jaundiced. Abdomen distended with shifting dullness. Bilateral leg edema.
Labs: creatinine 3.2 (1.0 a month ago per hospital records), BUN 45, sodium 130, potassium 4.5, albumin 2.8, INR 1.6. Urinalysis with minimal protein, no blood, no casts. AST and ALT mildly elevated; alkaline phosphatase normal.
Ultrasound: nodular liver, ascites, no biliary obstruction or hepatic vein thrombosis; TIPS patent.
ED course: diuretics held. IV albumin given; blood pressure did not meaningfully improve. Diagnostic paracentesis and blood cultures sent. Admitted to medicine with hepatology consult.

documents.title: Discharge summary: hepatorenal syndrome
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY — admitted 7/26/2026, discharged 8/4/2026. Received 8/7/2026.

Principal diagnosis: hepatorenal syndrome (acute kidney injury type) in decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis with ascites.

Hospital course: Creatinine 3.2 on arrival from a baseline of 1.0, bland urine sediment, no response to volume expansion with albumin; no shock and no nephrotoxins. Diagnostic paracentesis: ascitic neutrophils 110/uL, culture no growth — no spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Blood cultures no growth. Low-grade fever on arrival resolved without a source. Treated with terlipressin and IV albumin by hepatology with steady improvement; creatinine 1.9 on the day of discharge. Diuretics held throughout. He reports no alcohol since his February admission.

Discharge medications: testosterone cypionate 200 mg IM every 2 weeks, vitamin K 10 mg daily, lactulose 30 mL BID PRN. HOLD furosemide and spironolactone until hepatology review. Propranolol remains stopped since TIPS.
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: hepatology clinic in 1 week with BMP; hepatology has placed a referral for liver transplant evaluation. Primary care follow-up recommended.

documents.title: Water pills
documents.author: patient
documents.body: I got out of the hospital last week, kidneys were bad. They told me to stop the water pills but the pharmacy just auto-filled them. Do I take them or not? Seeing the liver doctor Thursday.

documents.title: Re: Water pills
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Good question — don't take them. The hospital and your liver team want both the furosemide and the spironolactone held until they see you Thursday and check your kidney numbers. Keep the bottles; they may restart them. I read your hospital summary and saw they've started the transplant evaluation referral. Once you've seen them, please book a visit with me so we can get caught up.
